item.title: Gambonanza Early Board Money Guide - How to Farm Stock Fast on a 5x5 Opening Board
item.description:
The Opening Board Is Your Real Money Engine

The Short Version

Every Gambonanza run starts on a 5x5 board with 3 pieces, and every board growth step only happens after you beat a boss checkpoint. That means the first several games of any run are played on a small, cramped board, and that cramped board is also where your economy is most fragile. Farming Stock here is not about a secret opener. It is about understanding that you earn money for winning games, and then spending that money correctly in the shop. The Economy Guide covers the full investment picture, and the Board Size Strategy Guide explains why small boards change your build.

item.title: Gambonanza Money Guide - Where Gold Comes From and What to Buy
item.description:
The Economy, Without the Noise

THE SHORT VERSION

Gold comes from winning games, Gold Tiles, and specific Gambits. There are no investment tables, no compound interest, and no hidden catch-up mechanic. A healthy run is one where you can afford one good buy per shop and still have a buffer for a bad boss fight.

Where Your Money Comes From

Source How it works
Winning a game The main source. You earn gold for capturing every enemy piece
Gold Tiles Landing a piece on a Gold Tile pays out
Gold Gambits A few Gambits convert captures or landings into gold
Selling a Gambit You can sell a Gambit you no longer use to recover part of its cost
Pro tip:
The real economy rule
You cannot farm gold forever. Crumble and the Stalemate Counter keep games moving, so every turn spent stalling is a turn you could be capturing and earning. Economy and tempo are the same skill in this game.

How the Shop Works

Every shop offers a fixed layout. Read it before you spend.

item.title: Stage 4 Economy Wall - 3 Reasons Your Gold Dies Before the Boss (and How to Fix Each)
item.description:
You reach Stage 4 with a healthy wallet and by the time the boss fight starts you are broke. I tested this exact scenario across many different builds, and I found the same pattern every time. The economy does not crash randomly. It crashes for three specific, preventable reasons that most players never diagnose. The Economy Guide covers this in depth. item.title: Yin & Yang Buffed to 1/2 in Gambonanza 1.4: Builds to Abuse
item.description:
The short version: Gambonanza 1.4.0 quietly turned three Gambits into real picks. Yin’s Gambit and Yang’s Gambit both moved from a 1/3 trigger to a 1/2 trigger, so they now fire noticeably more often. Rear Up’s Gambit went from +$2 to +$4 on promotion, which doubles the economy you get every time you promote a piece.

Run Yin and Yang together for steady triggers. Run Rear Up in any promotion build. Both are cheap, both scale with run length.

The Three Buffs at a Glance

Yin and Yang: 1/3 -> 1/2 trigger chance. Rear Up: +$2 -> +$4 per promotion. That is the whole headline.
Gambit Before After Impact
Yin’s Gambit 1/3 chance 1/2 chance Fires noticeably more often
Yang’s Gambit 1/3 chance 1/2 chance Same reliability bump
Rear Up’s Gambit +$2 per promotion +$4 per promotion Doubles promotion economy

The key point: Yin and Yang are triggers. Rear Up is economy. They solve different problems, which is why they pair cleanly.

item.title: Barter's Gambit Guide: Shop Reset Cycles & Graveyard Interaction (v1.5.1)
item.description:
EARLY GAME
Barter’s Gambit lets you sell a BISHOP and get another random piece in return, up to a limited number of times, resetting when you enter the Shop. The 1.5.1 hotfix adds a second reset: the trade also resets after a Graveyard. That makes Barter one of the more forgiving economy Gambits in the game, because two different systems now refresh your uses.
Barter’s reward is random, so the only thing you control is what you spend. If the Bishop anchors a diagonal your defense depends on, keep it and skip the trade.

What Barter’s Gambit Does

Barter’s Gambit is a trade engine. Selling a BISHOP grants you another random piece. The Gambit has a limited number of uses per cycle, and that cycle resets when you enter the Shop. The design intent is straightforward: turn a piece you do not need into a roll at a piece you might.

item.title: Stalemate Resets the Graveyard in Gambonanza 1.5.1: What Changed and Why It Matters
item.description:
MID GAME
As of 1.5.1, a Stalemate resets the Graveyard. Before, your list of lost pieces survived a Stalemate; now it is cleared. If you play PAWN difficulty and lean on recovery, this means your buyback list reflects only recent losses, not your whole run. Plan recoveries around Stalemate events instead of assuming old losses stay available.
As of 1.5.1 a Stalemate clears the Graveyard, so the window to buy back a key piece runs from the loss to the next Stalemate. Buy what matters before that window closes.

The Graveyard, in One Paragraph

The Graveyard is a PAWN-difficulty system introduced in v1.4.0. It holds the last five chess pieces you lost during a run, and you can spend money to buy them back. Each recovered piece raises the cost of the remaining ones, so recovery is a declining-value purchase rather than a flat fee. From KNIGHT upward, the Strain system removes the Graveyard entirely, because higher tiers are meant to make losses stick.

item.title: The Graveyard in Gambonanza 1.4: Recovering Lost Pieces & Buyback Cost Math
item.description: The Graveyard is a new piece-recovery system introduced in Gambonanza v1.4.0. It holds your last 5 lost pieces during a run, and lets you spend money to bring them back. Each piece you recover raises the cost of every remaining piece in the Graveyard, so the system punishes greedy recovery attempts while still giving you a genuine second chance. This guide covers exactly how the system works, how the cost escalation math plays out in practice, which pieces are worth buying back, and the design logic behind why it only appears on PAWN difficulty.

item.title: Gambonanza Build Guide - Core Directions and When to Pivot
item.description:
Not every direction works in every run. Good Gambonanza play is reading the shop and adapting. This guide covers the main directions, when each one works, and when to switch.

Do not force a build. Read what the shop and the boss preview give you, then commit. A flexible player with an average Gambit that fits their board beats a rigid player forcing a “best” Gambit they cannot trigger.

Direction 1: Tempo

Best for: Short, consistent games and any run where you want to end things before the counters matter.

item.title: Why Is My Stock Crashing? Economy Recovery Guide
item.description:
Stock Is Crashing \u2014 TL;DR

Stop. Don\u2019t play another Gambit until you diagnose.

If your stock is actively falling, it\u2019s not bad luck. It\u2019s one of: (1) a broken chain debt spiral, (2) a boss economy drain ability, or (3) passive decay from inactivity. Fix the cause before you play. Playing more Gambits into a broken system only accelerates the crash. The Economy Guide ranks every income option so you know which to prioritize during recovery. Emergency stock strategies are covered in the Emergency Salvage Guide.

item.title: Gambonanza Rook and Bishop Guide - When These Pieces Win Boards
item.description:
The Backbone, Not The Sidekick

Queen reaps the harvest. Rook and Bishop create the conditions for the harvest. But most beginners treat Rook as an expensive Pawn and Bishop as a budget Rook-this is completely backward. The Bosses Overview breaks this down in detail. The Strategy Guide breaks this down in detail.

Verdict

Rook is Gambonanza’s best value piece-moderate deployment cost, brutal suppression power, explosive Gambit synergy. Bishop is weaker man-for-man but irreplaceable in the right formations. Neither is a downgraded Queen-they’re complementary tools. Rating: A for Rook, B for Bishop (S-tier in the right formation).
